speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege of which I gave Your Honour notice a couple of hours ago. It is true that what I shall be saying arises out of events of the last few days concerning which there have been two or three interventions, but I assure Your Honour that I am now raising a new question of privilege, one that I believe affects every member of this House and also affects the working of this Parliament.
My question of privilege relates to the fact that it is now clear that when a crisis arises involving the unauthorized publication of a document that has been in the possession of the government, Parliament seems to have no recourse; there is nothing it can do to cope with the crisis. It is because we face this situation, and because it greatly hampers the working of this House of Commons, that I feel we should come to grips with this issue and call upon the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization to go into the matter and make a recommendation to the House.
[DOT] (2:10 p.m.)
In order to outline the situation, Mr. Speaker, may I take just a moment to remind Your Honour of what has happened. As everyone knows, when the present government came into power the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) laid down very strict rules regarding cabinet secrecy and made clear to his ministers what would happen if these rules were broken. For some time now we understand the cabinet has had possession of the report of the Le Dain commission but that the cabinet has kept possession of it on a secret and confidential basis. However, certain bits of information have leaked out and, as was indicated in a question of privilege at six o'clock last evening, Time magazine has published a report
which seems to be based on possession of the document or at least on possession of a summary of what is in the document. In other words, secrecy and confidentiality have been broken.
Now, sir, it seems to me this type of thing interferes with the efficient and proper working of a democratic institution such as this House of Commons. May I add, Mr. Speaker, that I think it interferes greatly with your position. I fully respect the rulings you have made on the interventions that have been raised in the last two or three days. I believe you have followed precisely our Standing Orders and procedures. Yet I think I would be less than honest if I were not to admit that Your Honour has looked uncomfortable because of the crisis which has been facing the House of Commons.
Your Honour has ruled against any motion under Standing Order 43 or any motion under privilege for the tabling of the report of the Le Dain commission. You have said that the only thing a member can do is to file a notice of motion for the production of papers, and Your Honour admitted from the Chair that at this stage of the game that is a rather unrealistic vehicle.
Your Honour has ruled against a request under privilege or under any other device for an inquiry into this whole matter which, as I say, is serious to us all. Personally, I well remember an incident of some 18 years ago. My friend the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) will remember it very well also. At that time there came into my possession the original version of a document known as the Currie report.

I suggest that this matter hangs like a cloud over Parliament and that it ought not to remain that way. However, I have already said I do not quarrel with the rulings Your Honour has given from the Chair. I may have presented argument on the other side but when Your Honour made the rulings I felt they were correct. But I think that in Parliament we ought not to find ourselves in this kind of a situation, frustrated as we are, when there is something in the nature of a crisis which affects the workings of Parliament. Yet we are asked to sit here helpless, unable to do anything about it. Instead of looking like the highest court of the land we are made to look like a barrel of monkeys.
I submit we should not be in this situation. There ought to be a way by which we can find out how this report came into the hands of Time magazine. We ought to be able to find out who was responsible. I suppose I should also say that we ought to be able to find out if Time magazine does have the correct report. It should not be made a matter of mystery and uncertainty, hanging like a cloud over Parliament.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, despite your rulings of the last few days that it is not a matter of privilege to refer to a committee the question of the source of this report in Time magazine and that it is not a matter of privilege to seek an inquiry into the whole matter, I do ask Your Honour to consider the difficult spot in which the House and you as our presiding officer are placed because of the fact that when a crisis of this kind develops there seems to be nothing we can do. If you find that in the name of Parliament I do have a prima facie case of privilege in what I have stated, I would then be prepared to move, seconded by my colleague, the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis):
That the lack of any redress on the part of the House of Commons when a confidential document in the possession of the government is made public without authorization be referred to the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization for consideration and report.

AVAILABILITY OF LE DAIN INTERIM REPORT TO "TIME" MAGAZINE-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION UNDER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. The matter I put forward does not relate directly to what the hon. member for Skeena raised a moment ago. The fact is that there is not yet a resolution before the House relating to the determination of the source of the cabinet leak. Standing Order 43 provides that in cases of urgent and pressing necessity a motion may be moved if unanimous consent is given. The matter of urgent and pressing necessity is the publication yesterday by Time magazine of purported extracts from the interim report of the Commission of Inquiry into the Non-Medical Use of Drugs.
This report has not yet been made available to members of this House and the public at large. It is, therefore, still a confidential cabinet document. By publication, cabinet confidentiality has been breached by someone in or close to the cabinet. At best this constitutes an unethical breach of parliamentary practice and at worst there may be illegality involved.
Therefore, under the provisions of Standing Order 43 I ask leave to move, seconded by the member for Skeena (Mr. Howard):
That this House is of the opinion that the government should conduct an immediate investigation to ascertain how the interim report of the Commission of Inquiry into the Non-Medical Use of Drugs came into the possession of Time magazine and to report its findings, either interim or final, to the House not later than June 26, 1970.

Mr. Speaker, I ask leave to move the adjournment of the House under Standing Order 43 in order to discuss immediately the emergency resolutions required on steps to be taken to remedy the situation of the Canadian footwear industry, which I consider very precarious.
Mr. Speaker, I feel that the study of this question justifies an emergency debate considering that since January 1, 1970 shoe factories have been closing down at the fantastic rate of nearly one a week and, considering that between 1956 and 1969, Canada's footwear production has decreased by 1 per cent whereas imports have jumped by 568 per cent, considering that the industry now employs 3,260 fewer workers than in 1966 and considering also that the government seems to have lost control of footwear imports into Canada.
Mr. Speaker, we all know that the unemployment rate depends mostly on the great number of unskilled workers on the labour market. Since a large number of employees of the footwear industry are in that category, I dare urge Your Honour to allow a debate to be held as soon as possible on ways to solve the pressing problem of that industry.
On June 2, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) announced to the House that talks were under way aboul restrictions of footwear imports and I believe the same measure is urgently needed regard ing the footwear industry.
I therefore ask Your Honour and hon members to consider, if possible, the motion to adjourn I am proposing to that effect.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: STATEMENT ON IMPLEMENTATION OF RECOMMENDATIONS OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, following the tabling of the third report of the Special Committee on Statutory Instruments, the government has made a full analysis of the impact of the recommendations in that report upon the many thousands of statutory orders and regulations issued by government and its agencies, and upon the procedures followed in preparing and reviewing regulations. The government has now determined a proposed course of action for responding to the report.
Due to the nature of the committee's recommendations it is not practical, nor is it reasonably possible, to proceed with their implementation by any one means. Rather, implementation of the committee's recommendations will require action of three different kinds: First, legislative action by Parliament to replace the existing Regulations Act by a new statutory instruments act; second, a number of cabinet directives to implement several of the recommendations which cannot be dealt with by general legislation and, third, amendment of the Standing Orders for the purpose of establishing a scrutiny committee to review regulations.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
The government accepts fully the principle that both Parliament and the public are entitled to be fully informed of, and to have convenient access to, regulations and other instruments made under the authority of Acts of Parliament. The legislation and other measures that will be proposed by the government will be guided by this paramount principle, and only demonstrably necessary and carefully defined exceptions to the general requirements of the law relating to the examination, registration and publication of such instruments will be permitted.
22478-26J
Statutory Instruments
The new statutory instruments act will update the present Regulations Act in light of the committee's recommendations. We will recommend that the definition of a regulation be expanded in order that certain subordinate legislation that is now excluded from the application of the present Act will come within the scope of the proposed new law. It will be proposed that the review procedure of proposed regulations that is conducted by the Clerk of the Privy Council in consultation with the Deputy Minister of Justice be given a statutory basis and that the fundamental principles in light of which the review is conducted be set forth in the legislation. A new system for registration of regulations will be provided and the date of registration will, in most cases, be the day on which a regulation will come into force. The Canada Gazette will be recognized by statute as the official gazette of Canada and powers to make regulations with respect to its publication will be provided. Other matters such as the requirements of the law to publish regulations and the right of members of the public to have access to and obtain copies of regulations will be dealt with in the new Act.
It is the intention of the government that the committee's recommendation No. 6 which is concerned with the publication of departmental directives and guidelines be dealt with by means of a cabinet directive. Departmental directives and guidelines that might reasonably be interpreted as affecting the rights of members of the public in a legal sense will be required to be submitted to the Deputy Minister of Justice before they are issued. The Deputy Minister of Justice will make a report to the person desiring to issue the document indicating whether the proposed directive or guideline is essentially legislative in its nature and, if so, whether it would be appropriate to incorporate it into regulations or, where there appears to be no authority to do so, whether the relevant statute should be revised with a view to conferring such authority.
With reference to the committee's recommendation No. 7, which is concerned with the general principles that should govern the conferring by legislation of regulation-making powers, a cabinet directive will be issued to all ministers directing that, in future, all such enabling legislation should be drafted in accordance with the principles proposed to the committee as acceptable to the government by letter dated September 30, 1969,

June 16, 1970
Statutory Instruments
addressed to the chairman of the committee and signed by myself as President of the Privy Council.
The government agrees with the general recommendation of the committee that a scrutiny committee should be established for the purpose of reviewing regulations. During the next session of Parliament the government will recommend that such a scrutiny committee be established and that by the proposed statutory instruments act all regulations, with the single exception of regulations the disclosure of which would be injurious to international relations, national defence security or federal-provincial relations, will stand permanently referred to such committee. After consultation with representatives of the parties, the government will put forward an order of reference in the next session to enable Parliament to establish a scrutiny committee.
Mr. Speaker, the limitations of a statement of this nature do not make it possible to give a detailed response to all of the committee's recommendations and, as a result, the foregoing is only a general outline of the manner in which we intend to implement the recommendations of that committee. In conclusion may I, on behalf of the government, express my gratitude to the chairman and members of the special committee for the contribution they have made by their report.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: STATEMENT ON IMPLEMENTATION OF RECOMMENDATIONS OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what the President of the Privy Council has said today bears out a maxim with which I became familiar in the early days of my practice of criminal law-that no matter how black the heart appears to be or how desperate the character there is always a glimmer of light and virtue if one waits long enough for it.
I congratulate the President of the Privy Council on making this statement. We have been waiting for it a long time, but obviously when it comes to good things the period of gestation of this government, like that of the elephant to which the Prime Minister refers from time to time, is very lengthy. For myself and for some others in the House it is the end of a ten-year period during which we have attempted to bring ourselves to a point at which we could hold up our heads and say that together with other democratic countries, particularly the countries of the Commonwealth, we have obtained some reasonable measure of ability to scrutinize statutory instruments and regulations.
[Mr. Macdonald (Rosedale) .1
This is a most essential thing that we do. The trend in modern legislative practice to delegate authority to the government is increasing. I know the reasons for it. I do not like it. But we have to live with it. We also have to learn to contend with it and place some brakes upon it, some means of scrutiny. We are happy, therefore, that the President of the Privy Council should indicate that the position taken by the government offers to be one of almost complete compliance with the report of the committee. The trend to which I have just referred has developed under this government and Parliament from what was a fair-sized river to a flood. The extent to which we in this House have been and are being asked to delegate to the government powers to deal with the people of this country is simply staggering, and precautions of the kind outlined today are a condition precedent to the maintenance to the kind of law and order for the individual which is needed in a democratic society.
There are one or two points I should like the government to take into account. It was proposed by the committee that the Minister of Justice should have over-all authority with regard to the examination of all regulations to decide whether or not they came within the category of those covered by the hon. gentleman's proposal. I appreciate that the minister was not able to deal with all the committee's proposals, which are minute and detailed, but the one to which I have just referred was among the main aspects which the committee considered.
Second, the question of the openness of disclosure is tremendously important. The minister told us in his statement, as found on page two, that "the government fully accepts the principle that both Parliament and the public are fully entitled to be fully informed of, and to have convenient access to, regulations and other instruments." I almost read "commission reports" into that as well but I am glad I stopped there.
In addition, the question of the establishment of a scrutiny committee is one with which the House should be particularly concerned. There is a scrutiny committee operating in other jurisdictions. There is a particularly good form of committee in the United Kingdom. I had the opportunity to attend the proceedings of that committee when I was in London not long ago. In the first instance, in the United Kingdom the chairman is a member of the opposition. The chairmen of both the Public Accounts committee and of
June 16, 1970

the scrutiny committee dealing with delegated authority are both members of the opposition. I tried to get the special committee to go as far as that but was not altogether successful. The committee did say, however, that in order to make the objectivity of the committee apparent there should be some rotation among the parties as to the chairmanship. I do not know what the government intends to do in this regard, but if it does not go at least as far as the committee proposed the value of this work of scrutinizing regulations and so on will be seriously lessened.
Now a word about the kind of officials who should assist the committee. A great deal of work has to be done; there is a vast area to be covered. In the United Kingdom Sir Robert Speed, counsel to Mr. Speaker, advises the committee and examines all the statutory instruments closely. In the absence of assistance of this kind, the value of the committee will be entirely lost. Assistance must be given at a very high level in order that it may function properly. There must be adequate staff.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
I particularly call to the attention of the government and members of the House the need not only to deal, as the committee did, with academics and people learned in the law but to hear from those people of the country, the millions of little people, businessmen and farmers, who are affected by delegated legislation and authority. These people do not know what Orders in Council have been passed and are not aware of them until the long arm of the law reaches out and touches them.
This is a tremendously important step and on behalf of myself and my party may I say that if the government will co-operate with us we will co-operate with the government 100 per cent in seeing that these proposals are implemented in an orderly and reasonable fashion. In particular, we will see that the type of committee set up to scrutinize statutory legislation is one that will function efficiently and properly, one that will do for the people of this country that which for so long has been left undone.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: STATEMENT ON IMPLEMENTATION OF RECOMMENDATIONS OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my colleague the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) was our member on the committee, the report of which is referred to in the statement, and if he were here today he would be making this response. He did not get permission under
Statutory Instruments
Standing Order 5 to be away, but it is interesting that by coincidence he is appearing before the Immigration Appeal Board which deals with matters that arise as a result of the exercise by a department of delegated authority. When I showed the advance copy of the statement to my colleague this morning, his comment was not unlike that which has just been made by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), namely, that once in a while something good does come from the government now in power. This is one of those rare occasions.
We welcome the statement by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Macdonald) that the government is prepared to implement the basic principles of the report made by the committee on statutory instruments. I support the general principles that have been laid down so well by the hon. member for Peace River, and we look forward to the promised legislation being introduced as early as possible.
There are just two or three comments 1 should like to make which might be of a critical nature. First, we find it strange that regulations dealing with federal-provincial relations should be put in the same category as regulations dealing with international relations or national defence security. We see no reason why these matters should be grouped together. Surely our provinces are not sovereign states to be treated like foreign powers. Surely relations between Ottawa and the provinces can be carried on on the kind of level that would produce regulations which would not be injurious to the unity of this country. We strongly urge that regulations relating to federal-provincial relations be deleted from this category.
The second comment I should like to make is that in this statement made by the President of the Privy Council there are two references, but only two, to cabinet directives that are to be made governing certain aspects of this whole process. If the picture were one of multitudes of things that had to be dealt with by cabinet directives, then maybe a case could be made for it. But if there are only two matters under this general heading that are to be dealt with by means of a cabinet directive, I suggest it would be far better to have those matters dealt with in the legislation itself.
My final comment is that it seems to me that the scrutiny committee which is to be established-this is the heart of the whole

June 16, 1970
Statutory Instruments
matter, the part of the statement that we welcome most-should have referred to it just not Orders in Council and regulations but also the various departmental directives that are promulgated down the line. These directives can have the force of law just as much as regulations, Orders in Council or statutes of Parliament. We find it difficult to understand why they are not included among the items which will be referred to the scrutiny committee. In this regard I might go one step farther and say that ministerial press releases could also be referred to the scrutiny committee, because many a time a ministerial press release relating to something that is going to be done is practically a case of promulgating law.
These points can, of course, be reviewed when the government presents the legislation, I presume at the next session. However, our general position is one of welcoming this forward step in the control by Parliament of the law-making process, which is as it ought to be.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON IMPLEMENTATION OF RECOMMENDATIONS OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are satisfied with the announcement of the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Macdonald) who just told us of the decision of the government to accept the recommendations concerning the proceedings of committees and the recommendations of the Committee on Procedure and Organization, which has been sitting for months, in order to suggest to the government the use of more flexible methods to formulate laws and let the public know about them.
Mr. Speaker, I would not like to repeat here the proposals of the previous speakers, but we entertain doubts as to the future formulation of laws, as a result of the recommendations made to the government after consideration in committee, the object of which is to give wider powers to the executive.
At the present time, we do not know to what extent this legislation will interfere with our democratic institutions and increase the powers of the executive. In fact, we are well aware that time and again in the past we have had to deplore the attitude of certain ministers who announced the tabling of legislative measures of which committees had had no prior knowledge and of which hon. members were only informed at the time the bills were tabled.

We are convinced that certain recommendations must be accepted but we also believe that some of them must be very seriously considered before they are submitted to Parliament and eventually incorporated to our Standing Orders so that debating and legislating procedures have to conform to them.

subtopic: CANADA LABOUR (STANDARDS) CODE INCREASE IN MINIMUM HOURLY WAGE

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: The House proceeded to the consideration of Bill C-214, to amend the Canada Labour (Standards) Code, as reported (without amendment) from the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration.

speakeroldname: Mr. Sianley Knowles (Winnipeg North Centre) moved:
speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: CANADA LABOUR (STANDARDS) CODE INCREASE IN MINIMUM HOURLY WAGE
speechtext:
That Bill C-214, an Act to amend the Canada Labour (Standards) Code, be amended by deleting from lines 12 and 13 thereof the words "one dollar and sixty-five cents", and by substituting therefor the words "two dollars".
He said: It is not my intention to provoke a lengthy debate on the amendment which has now been placed before the House but I hope hon. members will be prepared to accept it and thus make a significant improvement in the bill which has been brought in by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey). Having said that in my view a prolonged debate at this stage is unnecessary, I shall not repeat the arguments I used when we discussed this bill on second reading on May 29, although I should like to use again one or two of the arguments I advanced when the bill was before the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration.
As hon. members are aware, the bill is a very simple one in that it makes just one change in the Canada Labour (Standards) Code. It proposes that the minimum wage stipulated in the Code, which is now $1.25 an hour, should be made $1.65 an hour. My amendment proposes that, instead, the minimum wage be set at $2 an hour. As we all realize, this is a statute which applies to workers who come under federal labour jurisdiction. It does not apply to the federal public service but rather to workers such as railway employees, communications workers, bank employees and the like who, under the terms of the British North America Act, come under federal labour jurisdiction. There are about
550,000	workers in Canada who find themselves in these various categories but of course the number affected by any minimum wage provision is very low, since many of them have better arrangements as a result of collective bargaining agreements.
I must, however, correct the figure I gave on May 29 when I said I thought there were
June 16, 1970	COMMONS
probably fewer than 10,000 people who would
be affected by this bill-that there were fewer than 10,000 of the 550,000 whose wages were so low that they would get an improvement if their wages were brought up to $1.65 an hour. I now find from figures which the Department of Labour has been good enough to furnish to us that the number may be as high as 20,000. Previously, I estimated that only 2 per cent of those under federal jurisdiction were affected; the figure may turn out to be closer to 4 per cent. Since this larger number of people would be affected by the legislation, it is all the more important that we should do the right thing by them.
I said earlier that I will refrain from repeating the arguments I used on second reading. But when we got into the committee there were two points which I sought to make, and I beg the indulgence of the House to make them here as well. I shall try to make them a little more effectively than I did there, in the hope that we can go just a step further. In the committee, when I moved my amendment there and it came to a vote, a tie resulted and the chairman had to decide by his casting vote that the bill should remain as drafted. I hope this will not happen today. I hope you will not be put in that awkward situation, Mr. Speaker. I hope that instead of a tie there will be a clear majority in favour of my amendment.
The first of the new arguments I used in committee involved quoting an authority we in this party do not often put in that category. I refer to Dr. John Young, the chairman of the Prices and Incomes Commission. But even people who hold ideas with which we do not agree can, at times, have ideas which are correct. I remind hon. members that when Dr. Young issued his statement at the famous weekend meeting in Winnipeg calling for restraint in terms of there being no wage increases allowed beyond 6 per cent, he said very clearly that there were certain groups of people to whom this should not apply. One of these groups consisted of those earning less than $2 an hour. In other words, Dr. Young recognized that anyone whose wage was below $2 an hour could, notwithstanding the policy of the Prices and Incomes Commission, have that wage brought up to $2 an hour. The proposed restraint does not apply. Anything less than $2 is so low that even Dr. Young would not object to its being brought up to the figure I propose.
Surely, with all this support the government is giving to Dr. Young in connection
DEBATES	8169
Canada Labour (Standards) Code with the negative proposals he has made, the minister and his colleagues will also go along with his more positive suggestion, namely, that no wage below $2 an hour should be tolerated at all. I, therefore, call upon the Minister of Labour to help avoid the possibility of a tie, should the amendment come to a vote, by throwing his weight behind my proposal and helping to improve the position of those who are governed by the minimum wage under the Canada Labour (Standards) Code.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
The other argument which I introduced in the standing committee was one to which a colleague of mine alluded in a question that he asked during the question period yesterday relating to an example of some of the people who are getting these low wages. I confess that I was astounded when I got these figures from the Department of Labour setting out the numbers of people who are drawing wages that work out to less than $1.65 an hour. Believe it or not, Mr. Speaker, but of the 20,747 people who in June 1969 were drawing less than $1.65 an hour, 8,000 were employees of the chartered banks of this country. In other words, 40 per cent of the employees in this lower bracket are employees of the banks of this country.

subtopic: CANADA LABOUR (STANDARDS) CODE INCREASE IN MINIMUM HOURLY WAGE
speechtext: Shame.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: CANADA LABOUR (STANDARDS) CODE INCREASE IN MINIMUM HOURLY WAGE
speechtext:
The
chairman of the Prices and Incomes Commission has finally twigged to the inconsistency of some of the things that the banks are saying and doing by calling for an investigation into the profits of banks. A report in the Globe and Mail a few days ago carried the headline "Major banks show $275.2 million profit". That is covered by another heading which reads "27.7 per cent first half rise". That is their increase in profits in the first half of their fiscal year. If the banks of this country are making profits that run into these many millions, profits that in terms of percentage shoot high, wide and handsome through any guidelines talked about by the Prices and Incomes Commission, I suggest it is downright immoral for these people to be paying wages of less than $1.65 an hour to
8,000	of its employees. There just is no defence for this whatsoever.
By the same token, I submit that the government has no defence if it does nothing about this. All that the government has to do to correct this situation is to accept the
June 16, 1970

Canada Labour (Standards) Code amendment now before the House in my name calling for a minimum wage of $2 an hour, for all those who come under federal labour jurisdiction. In that instance, these
8,000	people would get their wages increased to $2 an hour, and there are probably a few hundred or thousand between $1.65 and $2 an hour who would also get an increase to that figure.
Not only are there the 8,000 bank employees to whom I have referred, who are receiving a starvation wage, but there are 5,675 persons in the transport industries who are receiving less than $1.65 an hour. I have grouped together several branches of transport, covering railway, air, road and water transport services. For the most part, workers in our transportation industries are covered by collective agreements, and most of the workers in those industries are doing better than $1.65 an hour. But these employees are persons in non-scheduled positions of various kinds, and there are some 5,675 of them whose present wage is less than $1.65 an hour. I should qualify the word "present" by saying that the figures I have are the latest I could get from the Department of Labour and are for June 1969. Although there may have been some improvement since, I am sure the situation has not been rectified to any great extent.
In addition, we have been told that the radio and television industries are not exactly on the rocks; that if you can get a licence to run a radio or a television station, in effect it is a licence to print money. Yet in radio and television in this country there were in June, 1969, 860 people who were receiving wages that worked out to less than $1.65 an hour. I do not think we should stand for this another day or even another afternoon.
I think there should not be any question at all about my amendment this afternoon. The House should say to the banks, to the transport industries and to the radio and television licensees that the least they must do is to bring their employees up to $2 an hour. The minimum wage proposed by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) of $1.65 an hour, for a person who manges to work 40 hours a week, 52 weeks in the year, would work out to $3,432. The Economic Council of Canada has selected the sum or $4,200 as the poverty line for an employee with a family today, so to say to these people that they should get by on $3,400 is selling them short by $800.
This is what this bill in the name of the minister would do, that is, unless my amend-

ment were accepted. If the amendment were accepted, it still would not bring affluence to these people. A wage of $2 an hour would mean, working 40 hours a week 52 weeks of the year, an annual wage of $4,160, which is at least within $40 of the poverty line indicated by the Economic Council of Canada. I have used 52 weeks in those figures to get the maximum amount in both cases, but I would hope that the provisions relating to vacations with pay would also apply to these people, that some of the employers who are getting away with these low wages are not at the same time getting away with practices that deny vacations to these employees.
There it is, Mr. Speaker; it is a simple proposition. I see no reason at all for the House not accepting this amendment of mine this afternoon. I know, of course, that we will be handed the usual arguments. The minister will tell us that he is trying to be realistic. I get awfully fed up with this line about having to be realistic. What about those people who are trying to live on this sort of money? What about realism for them?
I know the minister will also tell us that we have to be careful; that this matter involves the provinces as well as the question of whether industries will move from one province to another, or move from Canada to some other country; that we have to look at all these things; that we have to find some sophisticated ways to cope with the problem of poverty; that we must concern ourselves about the question of regional disparity and all that sort of thing; that maybe we will have to look at the situation of the banks as distinct from the situation of other industries. But after all these arguments have been put, we come back to the simple fact that this afternoon we are dealing with some 20,000 people employed in industries that come under federal labour jurisdiction and who are receiving less than $1.65 an hour. Probably some 22,000 or 25,000 or maybe more are receiving less than $2 an hour. I suggest that all of these arguments about federal-provincial relations, sophistication and realism do not apply.
The minister himself has said, and he said very effectively the other day in committee, that he is the kind of individual who is concerned about people. He did not claim anything for himself that he did not accord to the rest of us. But if we are all concerned about people, let us show our concern this afternoon by telling the minister that, yes, he has taken a good step by bringing in this bill to increase the minimum wage from that terribly low
June 16, 1970	COMMONS
figure of $1.25 an hour to a higher figure. But in the name of those people who are affected, and in a desire to be fair and to have some kind of just society, let us not stop there. Let us make it fair and reasonable. The other day one of the members of the committee complained about my amendment because he was afraid that if $2 an hour were agreed to this year, then in a year or two I would be asking for $3 or $4 an hour. I probably will be; in fact, I hope I will be. Progress does not stop. But it is not an answer to people who are living below the poverty line to tell them that for reasons of realism, of sophistication or of procedural difficulty, they have to stay at the same level.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
Mr. Speaker, the members of this House of Commons are sometimes shoved aside and sometimes feel irrelevant, but this afternoon we have the opportunity to act on behalf of
20,000	or 25,000 people. Therefore, I urge that this House support my motion, and by doing so let us raise the minimum wage in the Canada Labour (Standards) Code to the more reasonable level of $2 an hour.

Canada Labour (Standards) Code amendment and his speech on second reading or in committee the other day, nor will I attempt to come up with any different arguments in rebuttal. As I recall the debate on second reading, the one encouraging factor of course was the unanimous theme running through all the speeches made by members of all the parties in the House, including the Official Opposition, that there should and must be some increase in the minimum wages in this country. Had I viewed the minimum wage as the only instrument to alleviate poverty for certain classes of people, possibly I would have come up to $2. But when you are a minister charged with a certain responsibility you do not always have the freedom and flexibility that you may have in the opposition in taking into consideration one or two points.
Certainly, politically at least, it would be very palatable, so far as the relationship of the Minister of Labour and the government to
10,000	or 20,000 people is concerned, to bring in an amendment suggesting $3 an hour as the minimum wage. If I had that freedom, I would have proposed more than $2 an hour because it is certainly politically attractive. But as I mentioned on second reading and in committee, I have certain responsibilities and I have many other considerations which I thought I made as clear as possible.
We heard some very valuable contributions from representatives of the Atlantic provinces regarding the whole question of minimum wages. I think that in all the speeches on second reading some myths were dispelled which exist all too often in central Canada that the cost of living is so much lower in the Atlantic provinces. The fact that the people there can exist on a lower income is hardly a valid argument, but, as I pointed out earlier in the debate, I am opposed to the concept of regional minimum wages, either within a province or in a province within the nation.
So, in searching for a suitable figure, it became very obvious to me that I must come up with one that created the usual incentive, and the leadership with which the federal government has been associated ever since 1965 in establishing a minimum wage. I also had to establish a figure that did not create a distortion within a province or create unnecessary hardships for marginal industries, which may briefly be described as labour oriented rather than capital oriented. I was not unaware of the fact, through research in certain provinces, not necessarily the Atlantic provinces, that an increase in the
8172	COMMONS
Canada Labour (Standards) Code minimum wage even in the federal field could have perhaps induced a degree of rationalization in an industry which would be premature in the sense that in some cases it may have been economically advantageous to industries heavily dependent on machinery rather than labour before the regional expansion in that part of the country was sufficiently advanced to absorb displaced people.
I do have a responsibility not only to the employees but also to employers, and in many marginal industries dependent on labour rather than machinery we must take into consideration the effects which the minimum wage would have on their operation. I do not intend to refute any of the arguments which the hon. member brought forward with regard to chartered banks in this country and their ability to pay a living wage. It would seem to me that these banks would want to review their policy, taking into consideration their ability to pay, because I certainly do not consider the banks in this country to be marginal industries.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure all members of my party
June 16. 1970

Canada Labour (Standards) Code will agree when I say I am certain that the Minister ot Labour (Mr. Mackasey) would like to do the right thing. But, Mr. Speaker, the right thing is obviously not $1.65 per hour. I cannot believe that the minister was really serious when he said they arrived at $1.65 per hour through some kind of scientific study concerning productivity and the cost of living. I am inclined to take a much more political and pragmatic view of how they arrived at that figure, namely, that that was the highest figure the Minister of Labour could persuade his colleague, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) and a few other ministers, to accept. I point out that the President of the Treasury Board never had to worry about making a living, and that he represents the constituency of Westmount.
The minister talked about various other methods which can be adopted to raise the living standards of workers, particularly of unorganized workers who carry the main brunt of the low minimum wage. I agree with him that it is almost exclusively the unorganized workers who must live with the low minimum wage. But, Mr. Speaker, it is not much use to say to Canadian citizens, whether they live in Montreal, Winnipeg or Halifax, that some day in the future they will have pie in the sky, that some day in the future when the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) has worked out some of his beautiful plans, and the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) has worked out some of his plans and make the textile industry much more efficient than it is now, their wages will go up. Unfortunately, they have to live now, and as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) said, they have to live now on $1.25 an hour. Since the minister has rejected the $2 per hour suggested by my colleague, they will have to live on $1.65 per hour in the future.
The $1.65 per hour figure means that a married man with a family, if that is his wage, will receive an annual income which is $800 a year less than the Economic Council of Canada has set as the figure which divides those people who live in a state of poverty from those who live with some kind of decency. As I said on second reading, Mr. Speaker, this minister ought to be ashamed of himself for making such a niggardly proposal.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
I was glad to hear the minister substantiate the claims of members from the Atlantic provinces, and others such as my own, that

the cost of living is not much lower in the Atlantic provinces or Manitoba than in Ontario or Quebec. That simply reinforces the argument of those of us who say that the minimum wage, both federal and provincial, is too low and ought to be higher.
The last point I wish to deal with, and the one that brought me to my feet, is the suggestion or criticism-if it was a criticism- which the minister made of the government and the Premier of Manitoba because that government, which is NDP, had not moved immediately to a $2 minimum wage. The minister knows very well why that government has not moved. The minister knows that in every province there are marginal industries and if the minimum wage were increased in one province before another, it is likely those industries would be pushed out of business.
There is a very important garment industry in Manitoba. Most of the workers in that industry live in my constituency and that of my colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). The minister knows very well why the government of Manitoba has not unilaterally increased the minimum wage to $2 an hour, just as he knows that the minimum wage was increased to $1.50 on a temporary basis. It has been announced that it will probably be raised again in the fall. The government of Manitoba would like nothing better than to increase the minimum wage and I am sure that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) is aware of that, Mr. Speaker. But this cannot be done until other provinces with similar industries increase their minimum wage. It is for this reason I am so critical of the minister for this miserable increase he is proposing and which he wants us to support today.
Just speaking from memory and subject to error in some small detail, Mr. Speaker, I point out that when the federal minimum wage was set at $1.25 five years ago, no province had a minimum wage of more than 90 cents. We knew, of course, that there were not many employees coming under federal jurisdiction who were not receiving $1.25 then, just as there are not many employees coming under federal jurisdiction receiving less than $1.65 today. We knew, when the minimum was set at $1.25 five years ago, that the main effect of it would be to act as a spur on the provinces to increase their minimum wage and that is precisely what happened. The minimum wage in Manitoba is now $1.50 and I believe that in Quebec it will be $1.55
June 16, 1970

an hour by this fall. The minimum wage in every province has increased substantially since the legislation was passed five years ago. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that what was accomplished when the rate was set at $1.25 cannot be accomplished today when the rate is set at $1.65 because most of the provinces are already close to that rate. The benefits attained by the increase five years ago will not be attained today.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, we are including here a provision which is analogous to one already found in the Ontario, Quebec and Manitoba elections acts. What is involved here is really to provide a little flexibility for the Chief Electoral Officer where, for example, there happens to be a bomb scare in a polling booth, perhaps at five o'clock in the afternoon, and where as the result of safety precautions it may be necessary to clear the poll for several hours and therefore run the risk of disenfranchising a number of voters. It is subject to an over-all time limit so that the poll in total will not be open for a longer period of time, than is general under the act but this does permit that particular poll to remain open for a longer period of time than is usual. The discretion is exerciseable by the Chief Electoral Officer on the advice of the returning officer.

I realize we probably cannot cover every contingency and possibility here, but there is a provision elsewhere in the Act that no one shall publish the results of the election in one part of the country until the polls have closed in another part of the country, taking into account the time differences. Here we have a situation where a particular polling station in a particular polling division may be kept open beyond the normal closing time because of an emergency, or something unforeseen that may happen, in order to give the people in that polling division substitute time in which to cast their ballots. I am wondering whether the other provision relating to the sanction against publicizing the results of the election is included in this, or will it be permissible to publicize them in this instance? Will it be an infringement to publicize them if a polling station has to be kept open until midnight, or until three or four hours after the other stations close?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader

I think the over-all logic is that it would be difficult to hold up the whole country while two or three polls voted.

Then it goes on to the succeeding paragraph. The intention of this amendment is that when a writ had been withdrawn in an electoral district because of a disaster or emergency, the Chief Electoral Officer would cause a new writ to be ordered by the Governor in Council within three months, the writ to be returnable within three months after issue. In a general election the vacancy would be filled within six months, instead of taking six months to issue the writ and then whatever period was necessary after that to hold the election. I urge that this amendment be accepted because it seems more fitting and proper to conduct the election process in this manner, particularly in a general election when all electoral districts should be settled as early as possible.

Mr. Chairman, I have another amendment to present for the consideration of the committee. It would have the effect of adding a new subclause to clause 6. Many of us have been concerned over the years about the length of time it has taken to fill vacancies in Parliament. In years gone by vacancies were filled in a manner which nowadays would be considered nothing more than political chicanery or political manoeuvring. I think members of all parties agree that the electors of any electoral district have the right to be represented in Parliament at the earliest possible date following a vacancy in the House. I believe that no party in Canada, in this modern age, desires delay when vacancies are to be filled. I appreciate that on the death of an hon. member a reasonable period should be observed, out of respect for the member, before a writ is issued. That would be natural and courteous.
Having said that, Mr. Chairman, I think delays in the recent past have been longer than necessary. I do not ascribe any motives to the government. In the case of the former hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands, who died on July 10, 1968, subsequent to his election to the twenty-eighth Parliament, eight months passed before the vacancy was filled. In the case of the former hon. member for Selkirk, who resigned from this House and was successful in seeking opportunity elsewhere, 11 months passed before the vacancy was filled. At present a vacancy exists because a member of the Ralliement Creditiste resigned to sit in another chamber.
I urge upon the members of the committee an addition to this clause. I move:
That clause 6 be amended by adding thereto the following subclause:
"(6) Notwithstanding anything in this or any other act, where any vacancy happens in the House of Commons a writ ordering an election of a member of the House of Commons to fill such vacancy shall be issued within three months after the receipt by the Chief Electoral Officer of the warrant issued pursuant to the House of Commons Act, and that such writ be returnable within three months after issue."
I hope all members will favourably consider this amendment, Mr. Chairman. I know all of us would be interested in hearing the views of members from all parts of the chamber. I hope there is a general feeling that the day has long past when any government, of whatever party, would delay filling vacancies

in an electoral district at the expense of Canadians who would not have representation as soon as they should.

More fundamental, perhaps, is the fact that the House of Commons Act regulates this particular situation and the membership of the House of Commons as it is constituted from time to time.

Therefore, instead of making the change at this time we would be disposed to consider it in any future amendment to the House of Commons Act. Very likely, that measure will arise for consideration in the next session. We will, therefore, not make this change in the context of the bill now being discussed.

Mr. Chairman, I am not enthusiastic about the suggestion of the President of the Privy Council. He has merely said it is likely that the Senate and House of Commons Act will be amended in the next session. In view of the number of times we have been told it is likely that legislation apropos the Canada Development Corporation will come before the House, we take the minister's suggestion with a great deal of skepticism.
I would be more disposed to listen to the President of the Privy Council if he advanced some real arguments showing why the amendment of the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre is not now practical. Surely the minister does not want members of the House to think that the government needs freedom, for political reasons, not to call an election in any constituency for up to one year after a vacancy has occurred, and so leave that constituency unrepresented in this House. I have some experience of this situation. The former hon. member for Selkirk, who is now the Premier of Manitoba, asked me to look after certain matters relating to that constituency until the by-election could be held. I was happy to accommodate him, but I must admit that being a member who represents an

urban riding I found some difficulty in dealing with the difficulties raised by the farmers of the constituency of Selkirk.
The President of the Privy Council has not told us why any seat in this House should remain vacant for almost one year. The government may have political reasons; but I suggest to the minister that the democratic system being what it is, it is possible that the Liberal Party will not always form the government of Canada. There may come a time when it will be in opposition, and it will wish certain by-elections to be held even though the government of the day may not wish them to be held.
I suggest that we ought not to be playing politics in this kind of situation. We ought to enact rules saying that as soon as possible after a vacancy occurs, a by-election shall be held, no matter which party forms the government of the country. Therefore, if the minister has no political reasons for refusing the request of the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre, I urge him to accept the proposal of the hon. member.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, as I pointed out when replying to the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre who introduced this question, my reason for neither accepting nor rejecting the proposal put forward is that I think it should be considered in the over-all context of the House of Commons Act and not on the spur of the moment or in the manner now suggested. I would agree with the hon. member that it is patently obvious that the ability to postpone the holding of a by-election has not in any sense been of advantage to this government. The hon. member could characterize my reasons as political, but probably the sensible thing would be to deal with the matter within the context of the over-all statute and not to agree to this particular change at this time.

Mr. Chairman, I think the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre has brought forward a significant matter. This question has been dealt with in other jurisdictions. We seem to have developed a technique, if it is a technique, of prolonging vacancies. We have here a device whereby the executive arm of government is influencing improperly the composition of the legislative chamber. Other jurisdictions have, as a result of unfortunate experiences, found it expedient and wise to write into their laws provisions of the sort which the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre has brought forward.
June 16, 1970

While the suggestion may have been brought forward on the spur of the moment, in the eyes of the minister, the spirit of the suggestion is not at all new. I think events in this Parliament have served to underline the iniquity of our system whereby the executive, through inertia or other causes, can delay by-elections and thus the completion of the people's representation in Parliament.
I think any self-respecting government would wish to move as quickly as the law allows so that the people's parliamentary representatives may be installed in the lawmaking chamber. So I support the amendment, which I think would improve-and it is improvement that we are after-the efficacy of our system of representative government.

Mr. Chairman, may I join the mover of this amendment and my colleague the hon. member for Hillsborough in supporting this amendment. It seems that about every ten years we turn our attention in a substantive way to major changes to the Canada Elections Act. While I support the spirit of the Government House Leader's comments and think the matter ought to be looked at in the larger context, I hope the committee will not need to wait ten years for the consideration in that larger context to which he referred.

On clause 7, subclause 1-Appointment of returning officers.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, may I draw to the attention of the committee a related clause. I refer to clause 114(2) on page 198 of the bill which provides:
The Chief Electoral Officer, the Assistant Chief Electoral Officer and every other election officer appointed under the former act who held office immediately prior to the coming into force of this act shall continue to hold office with like effect as though they had been so appointed under this act.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
Under the previous Elections Act, the statute enacted in 1960, the positions of returning officers were declared vacant, for whatever use it was at that time. It is the considered
Canada Elections Act
opinion of the Chief Electoral Officer that, particularly in light of the change in the size of the electorate and the complications which would result from having to appoint 263 new returning officers, it would be desirable to keep in office those who have had experience. This preserves the positions of the returning officers.

What is the rate of pay for returning officers at the present time? I understand there is a retainer paid during years when there is no election, and a special rate during the time of an election. I also ask what procedures the Governor in Council follows when appointing people to fill vacancies in places where vacancies exist.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: A tariff of fees is established pursuant to clause 61(1) of the current bill. There is no fixed sum applicable to all returning officers; the amount depends upon the number of names on the electoral list and is determined during the course of each election. As to the second question, an attempt is made to appoint someone experienced in election procedures. The hon. member became a member of the House before I did, and no doubt he is familiar with the process on his side.
If that is an indication from the minister to make a recommendation to fill the vacancy in my constituency, I will gladly comply.

Mr. Chairman, I have an amendment to propose to clause 7(1). It proposes that returning officers should be appointed by the Chief Electoral Officer rather than by the Governor in Council. I make this suggestion as a result of my interest in the matter as well as on the basis of an exchange which took place in one of the earlier meetings of the Committee on Privileges and Elections at Which I was present. I should like to quote from the Minutes of Proceedings No. 2, dated October 31, 1968, beginning at page 8.
My question is supplementary to something Mr. MacGuigan said. He said that you and your office do not appoint the returning officers; that is done by the government.
That is correct.

You see, this brings up all kinds of interesting aspects of political patronage and that kind of thing in the appointment of these various returning officers, and I am interested in knowing what kind of recommendations you might have in this connection.

I do not have any recommendations. If you go back, I think to about 1930, the Chief Electoral Officer was responsible for the appoint-

June 16, 1970
Canada Elections Act
ment of the returning officers. I do not think this would be efficient because I do not have the machinery, having my office in Ottawa, if at the beginning of an election a returning officer drops dead or decides not to take the job away out in British Columbia, Alberta or in Saskatchewan, to try to find a replacement.
Do I understand, then, that the returning officers are appointed by the province or some organization within the province?

That I do not know.
Obviously, the Chief Electoral Officer has to reply officially. He does not know. The record continues:
How they go about getting their names, I do not know.

It seem very strange, sir, that no one knows something as vital and as basic as this and I just cannot conceive its happening. It is like the answer we got yesterday concerning the political affiliations of appointees. I am not laying this at the door of any one political party, because I think this certainly has happened under both of the major political parties, but I think we could certainly look to some other kind of method for appointing these people, because I am convinced that not always are the best people appointed for this purpose and further, that there have been some very capable ones who have been replaced regardless of the changing of the boundaries.
This is the amendment which I am proposing, Mr. Speaker:
That clause 7 be amended by deleting subclause 1 and substituting therefor the following:
"(1) The Chief Electoral Officer shall appoint a returning officer for any new electoral district, and a new returning officer for any electoral district in which the office of returning officer becomes vacant, within the meaning of subsection 2. Such vacancy to be filled after the Chief Electoral Officer has publicly advertised the vacancy, invited applications, and held open competition for the position."
I believe our civil service operates on the basis that vacancies are regularly published as they occur in the government service. In my opinion, this is an admirable method of procedure and I do not see why it cannot be followed in this instance when it concerns the staff of the Chief Electoral Officer. I am surprised that the government has not thought it wise to ensure that these appointments are made without any hint of patronage. In the past, capable people were removed and their positions given to government supporters who were not necessarily the most competent among the applicants.
These appointments offer a small crumb to some people, but one wonders why the government has not seen fit to remove the taint of party advantage from an area which is of vital concern to everyone in our democracy. I am not moving this motion because I have been personally wronged by

any electoral officer, but I believe the government should show confidence in its Chief Electoral Officer's competence to make appointments of this type impartially.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
