speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. House again in committee of the whole on Bill C-215, an act respecting the franchise of electors and the election of members to the House of Commons.
When the committee rose at six it was considering clause 7, subclause 1 and the following amendment moved by the hon. member for Fraser Valley West:
That clause 7 be amended by deleting subclause 1 and substituting therefor the following:
"(1) The Chief Electoral Officer shall appoint a returning officer for any new electoral district, and a new returning officer for any electoral district in which the office of returning officer becomes vacant, within the meaning of subsection 2. Such vacancy to be filled after the Chief Electoral Officer has publicly advertised the vacancy, invited applications, and held open competition for the position."

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when the hon. member for Fraser Valley West brought this amendment forward he referred at some length to an exchange that took place in the Standing Committee between himself and the Chief Electoral Officer, which seems to me probably the most effective answer to the points he was making at the time. As the Chief Electoral Officer pointed out, though I hesitate to quote him without reading his actual remarks, the system here appears to produce the most efficient way of appointing returning officers. It was also indicated at the time that up until about 1929 or 1930 they were appointed in the manner suggested by the hon. member. Then the House, nearly 40 years ago, changed the procedure so that they would be appointed by the Governor in Council and ever since that time this particular proposal has been in effect.
I understand it was the statement of a former Chief Electoral Officer, who operated under the older system, that the reinstitution of the system which in effect got him into controversy in a particular constituency by choosing the returning officer, would be a resigning matter as far as he was concerned. In other words, the law was changed specifi-
June 16, 1970

cally because of unhappy experience with the exact procedure that the hon. member is suggesting in this regard.
One other aspect of the hon. member's amendment which seems to me to be a good reason for recommending that the committee reject it is that there are other provisions in the statute-in particular subsection 5 of clause 7-for the purpose of the early filling of a vacancy, so there will not be a delay, and providing that the returning officer shall be appointed within 60 days. The procedure put forward by the hon. member, however, is a lengthy one with regard to which there can be no assurance whatever that within 60 days, or at any particular time, a vacancy would be filled. In other words, in order to carry out the procedure proposed by the hon. member, a particular constituency could find itself several weeks before an election campaign without a returning officer, and because of the restrictions that he imposes, without the ability of appointing one at an early date.
On that basis, Mr. Chairman, both because Parliament long ago rejected the proposal and because it will not provide, to adopt a term that has been used, for the efficiency of appointment, I recommend to the committee that it reject this amendment.

Mr. Chairman, I think it is of the essence that every way we can find to reduce even the suggestion of partisan input into our election procedures should be welcomed. I am somewhat attracted to the proposal of the mover of this amendment. I notice that in several sections of the bill steps have been taken to put beyond question or reproach even any slight suggestion of partisanship. In the holding of an election, surely any distinction between a party in power and a party seeking power must be removed just as completely as is possible in all practical circumstances. I think it is well that we consider ways and means to reduce even the possibility of accusing a group in power of using the fact that they are in power for purposes other than the best purposes.
I am not suggesting that in our day and age elections have not been well conducted in this country, though in an earlier day that was not the case. I remember reading of an experience in the nineteenth century when nominations were made at an open meeting. The sheriff of one county did not tell the opposition party where the meeting was going to be held, and there was no one there to nominate the opposition candidates. As a result, there was an acclamation. However,
Canada Elections Act
things have been much better in recent times. If we could move toward de-politicizing-if I may use a terrible expression-our election campaigns to this extent, it would be a very good idea. When enumerators are appointed, the whole matter is carefully looked into; you have one designated by one party and one by another, so there is an assurance that you have reduced to the minimum any possible suggestion of partisanship. If we could do this with the returning officer, I think it would be a very good idea.
If I remember history correctly, I think at the time of the plebiscite that Mr. Mackenzie King called there was a procedure whereby in odd numbered polling divisions the deputy returning officer was the nominee of the government party, and in even numbered polling divisions he was the designate of the second running party. These are devices whereby you establish a good, proper, non-political basis which is of the essence in our electoral process. This is my point of view, and I support the amendment.
The minister was dilating this afternoon about the value of experience in the office of returning officer. Before we proceed further with this clause I wonder whether he could tell us how many of the returning officers who were appointed in the aftermath of the 1960 legislation are still functioning, because I agree with him that there is value in the experience of good people.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)

Mr. Chairman, before we become involved in the de-politicizing, or whatever the term is, let me make some comments in the privacy of this House. I see we have complete privacy because there is no one to report us. Let us consider what the result of this amendment would be. The Chief Electoral Officer would be very careful not to choose anyone with political ideals either Conservative, Liberal or NDP. This would automatically eliminate about 80 per cent of the people who know something about politics and about the running of elections. The Chief Electoral Officer would look for someone who had never been involved in political activity of any nature and who did not know a poll sheet from any other document. Such a person would have to be trained. This is the type of person who would be a returning officer.
In addition, about five years ago the Prime Minister decided it would be a good idea to take patronage completely away from all appointments. Where did we turn? We could

June 16, 1970
Canada Elections Act
not go to the general field of economics or industry in order to find people, because they were involved politically with the Liberal Party, the Conservative Party or the NDP. It was decided that academicians of the universities would be suitable because no one could say that they were partisan. Eventually the various commission appointments were filled by academicians-good natured souls, mind you, but people who have very little experience in the outside world. So in their little Valhalla they set down rules which in theory are perfect but which in practice have no application at all. Why should we penalize anyone who has been involved in political activity? What has such a person done that would warrant his being eliminated entirely?
No one suggested that.

That is what an hon. gentleman across the way said. He said we should take politics away from these appointments. It was suggested that if a person is to be appointed as a judge, a commissioner, a returning officer, and so on, he should never take part in politics. In other words, the suggestion is: Never vote. Do not become involved. This is in fact what has been said.
I say it is time we reviewed this whole question. I see nothing evil in being involved with one political party or another. I can conceive of the Governor in Council obtaining an even better group of men from those who have been involved in politics than from those who have not.

Mr. Chairman, I feel obliged to reply to the arguments put before the committee by the hon. member who has just spoken because he is drawing from this amendment a conclusion which should not be drawn. Such an interpretation has no place in our discussion of the amendment. The sole purpose of the amendment is to ensure that the most competent people are selected to fill the position of returning officer. For obvious reasons, this would not eliminate a person merely because he had been involved in politics. Indeed, I think any intelligent Chief Electoral Officer would consider intimate involvement in politics to be a "plus" factor in the selection of a returning officer.
This amendment does not in any way indicate that a person must be non-partisan. It simply indicates that he must acquire the position as a result of an open competition. What it does mean is that if there should be a Liberal government in office, all the returning

officers would not be former Liberals; and if there should be a Conservative government in office, all the returning officers would not be former Conservatives. Similarly, if an NDP government should be in office, all the returning officers would not be members of the New Democratic Party. It simply means that there would be a competition and the most competent applicant would fill the position. That is the point; anything else is totally irrelevant to the question. On that basis I urge the committee to adopt this amendment.

Mr. Chairman, I thank the hon. member for Selkirk for apologizing, on my behalf, for things I did not say and for interpretations I did not mean. No one is suggesting that the appointees be political neuters: they must become that, because the law does not allow them to vote when the poll is open. I was suggesting that politicizing be withdrawn from the appointing product rather than from the end product. I do not agree that one must be partisan in order to be competent. I can conceive of the independent voters managing the Elections Act, too.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. I will recognize the hon. member after the hon. member for Fraser Valley West.

Mr. Chairman, I would gladly withdraw if I could be the last speaker. The hon. member would then have my permission to go ahead, but in the event that committee of the whole procedure precludes this kind of generosity, I should like to proceed. It seems to me that the arguments against my amendment have been approached from the wrong premise. I do not accept the type of argument rendered by the hon. member for York East, to the effect that my amendment means that people who have taken an active interest in politics should by virtue of their interest be precluded.
We are interested in obtaining the best possible people to fill the position of returning officer. My concern is that the best possible people be appointed by the government for the position of returning officer. I feel that the fact the government is involved in various partisan considerations might tend to make it appoint persons who are favourable to its political party.
Essentially, I am asking that there be an open type of competition in which people who have been involved in partisan politics
June 16. 1970

from the point of view of scrutineer, enumerator, returning officer, and so on, would have a free hand in submitting applications to the Chief Electoral Officer for consideration by him in his wisdom, intelligence and great experience in dealing with this type of person, rather than the appointment being made through the Governor in Council.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to support the amendment, but I am not so naive as to believe that over the years governments have amended the act so that they could obtain returning officers who were more favourable to their own cause. Let us get down to brass tacks. What we need is something exactly like the amendment now before the committee. This situation is similar to that in respect of redistribution. That is something I always oppose.
It was said that judges should be appointed to the redistribution commissions because they were independent persons. Unfortunately, in various areas judges were politicians before they became judges. Therefore, we had as much politics in redistribution as we would have had had we turned the matter over to a committee of the Senate and House of Commons. If any member should stand in his place now and suggest that parties do not play politics with regard to this act, in relation to returning officers, they should examine their own conscience or their own people. They have all been playing politics. The NDP have not been in office federally, but they were in office in my home province and I did not see any non-politics there.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
You should see them in Manitoba.

Mr. Chairman, I would join the hon. member for Calgary North in expressing a comment or two about this amendment. I am one of those who admit to being a political animal from time to time. But I am one of those who-I have no hesitation in confessing it-in the few years that I have been here have found it a lot more enjoyable to work for people for all but two months of the four or five years that a government is in office, and at that time to be a little political.
While I support this amendment-I have no hesitation in doing so, largely for the reasons enumerated by my colleague-I think that in fairness it should be brought to the attention of the committee, its acceptance would give rise to serious questions about other procedures under the act. It is to the other procedures that I should like to direct my attention: not only to the procedure that involves partisan politics in the selection of returning officers and their clerks, but to the entire procedure to which we must direct our attention from 1970 onward.
I am not about to say that political appointees are not competent. I hope I misunderstood my hon. friend when he expressed what I understood to be that opinion, because I believe that regardless of their political beliefs, when people are considered for roles such as this they are by and large competent. But what is important is that we do not strip-I simply mention this for what it is worth-the political process in Canada of the means of adequately prosecuting general elections.
The point has been made by the minister, and I think validly so, that there are times when the returning officers must seek local advice. It is not always possible at the eleventh hour for the returning officer responsible for the prosecution of an election in a given electoral district to secure the required replacement, if that is what the problem is, and he must turn to somebody for advice and

June 16, 1970
Canada Elections Act
direction. There is not always time the day before the election to run an advertisement in a newspaper and to secure a list of candidates from which he can select an appropriate returning officer.
I draw this matter to the attention of the committee, and at the same time I run the risk of being contradictory when I say that notwithstanding this very apparent difficulty and the very difficult position in which we might place the Chief Electoral Officer, and indeed the voters in a given riding, it is perhaps time, in 1970, that we devised a more efficient way of securing the appropriate officers who are required to prosecute elections.
The amendment very clearly has merit. I only hope that in the wisdom of the chamber, if we decide to accept the amendment we will look with charity at consequential amendments that will have to be made, some of which will be moved by myself. I commend the amendment to the committee. I do so on the basis of 14 or 15 years' experience of dealing directly with these matters. The matter should be taken out of the hands of political organizations, because this is in fact what we are talking about.
It does not matter how much we try to hide it, it does not matter how much we try to get around the basic fact of the matter: what happens in truth is well known to all of us, and in many instances has caused some of us who have had responsibility in running elections, both on our own behalf and in assisting others, considerable difficulty, particularly during the latter stages of general election campaigns. I sincerely urge hon. members who are here tonight to reflect for a moment or two on the merit of this amendment. If in their wisdom they decide that it should be rejected, I ask each of them individually to make a plea to the Government House Leader who is responsible for the passage of this bill to make sure that this item is included in the promised review for this fall.

Mr. Chairman,
before we proceed with the amendment indicated by the hon. member for Fraser Valley West, I rise on a matter of order. I do so in a very expansive and generous way, to point out that the Chief Electoral Officer is in reality, as I understand it, an officer of Parliament and not an officer in the sense that a member of the public service is an officer attached to a particular department.
It is true that the Chief Electoral Officer is here on the floor of this House. I have some doubt about the propriety of that, but that is another matter. He is here with a very attractive young lady whose position I do not know so far as the Chief Electoral Officer is concerned. The question I want to raise is that the office of the Chief Electoral Officer being one of Parliament, it should not be one, just by proximity to the President of the Privy
Canada Elections Act
Council, to be in any way considered as a position seconded to the President of the Privy Council as a member of the cabinet.
I am sure that Mr. Hamel and the office of the Chief Electoral Officer are available during tonight's sitting, as was the case this afternoon, to any member who wants to consult them about the technicalities, legalities and other details of anything involved in this legislation. But I think that this office and its facilities, being an office of Parliament and not a partisan one-not attached to government or opposition-should be available to opposition groups who are as concerned as the government about developing the Elections Act so that it will meet the requirements and the needs of the people of this nation in their election of Members of Parliament.
I do not know whether we could arrive at some arrangement in this respect. I realize that the Chief Electoral Officer cannot be jumping from one party to another in the developing of amendments and in suggestions about them, but the office of the Chief Electoral Officer should be available to all parties and all groups in this House as easily as it is to the President of the Privy Council at the moment.
Whether it is possible to work this out at the moment, I do not know. There may be some technicalities involved in doing so. But I think it is incumbent upon us in this House, and upon you, Mr. Chairman, to look upon this question as having great validity. The hon. member for Hillsborough and the people associated with him in the Conservative Party who have spent a fair amount of time over the years, before many members came to this House, dealing with electoral reform and the Elections Act, should have available to him and to the group associated with him the expertise and knowledge that exists within the office of the Chief Electoral Officer. My friend from Regina-Lake Centre should not have to rely upon the highly incompetent legal advice that he says he gets from myself and from the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. He should be able to draw on something much more knowledgeable than that. I raise the point and leave it with the committee for comment. I think it is a very worth-while point that we should consider.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would like to make it perfectly clear, on behalf of the Chief Electoral Officer, that the opinion of the hon. member for Skeena is correct, that he is an officer of Parliament

June 18, 1970
Canada Elections Act
and that he is and will be available to all hon. members from time to time as they may need assistance. In terms of physical mobility around the floor of the chamber, I am open to suggestions as to how he could be made more available than he is now. But I am advised that the procedure now being followed, with the Chief Electoral Officer advising the minister who is conducting the passage of the bill, was the procedure followed when the House last had the Elections Act before it in 1960, and it was the practice followed in years before that. So I would make it perfectly clear that he is not the exclusive adviser of the government. If there are to be amendments which may involve technical advice on their consequential effect on other parts of the act, I think it might be necessary to postpone them. The second point which I raised, and which the hon. member has not considered, is that an open competition of this kind, particularly in circumstances where a quick appointment may be necessary, will not be effective and could well leave one or more constituencies without returning officers. Under the system which is in vogue we have the advantage, as the Chief Electoral Officer pointed out in the passage taken from the proceedings of the committee which the hon. member read, that we can efficiently fill vacancies when, as is often the case, there is a great rush, and thus make certain that each constituency has a returning officer before an election is held.
It seems to me that the amendment meets neither of the two points I raised earlier. It does not really deal with those two substantial objections, both of which arise on the basis of experience accepted by this House, which has been the basis of the Elections Act for some time.

Mr. Speaker, I would support the amendment that has been moved by my hon. friend for Fraser Valley West because I think it represents the sort of compromise that is required if we are to circumvent the sensitivity that is involved in straight political appointments of this kind. The President of the Privy Council has indicated that the Chief Electoral Officer is not anxious to become involved in the process of appointing returning officers. As I understand it, under the compromise amendment put forward by the hon. member for Fraser Valley West, the ultimate responsibility lies in the hands of the Governor in Council and the Chief Electoral Officer would only be acting in an advisory capacity.
Speaking as one who has experienced eight elections, I can confirm the fact that the role of returning officer is of vital importance in ensuring the proper and efficient conduct of an election campaign. It seems to me that the Chief Electoral Officer, who has had very
June 16, 1970

close association with the returning officers and, through them, with the candidates in the constituencies of Canada, might be able to channel the experience that has been gained by those who have participated in elections by ensuring that each candidate involved in the electoral process, or the representative of each of the parties contesting a constituency in an election, is consulted. In that way they could make recommendations as to who might be the most suitable person to handle this very sensitive task. This, I think, would get around the problem which concerns all hon. members with regard to clause 7. There is an amendment which indicates that the office is now to be made permanent, subject to certain reservations. I think this is an excellent compromise. Mr. Chairman, I rise to add what I hope will be some reasonably convincing words in support of the motion moved by the hon. member for Fraser Valley West, and favourable to what we regard as a compromise more acceptable to the President of the Privy Council than the motion we moved earlier. In reality, under the terms of this amendment, the Governor in Council still has the final say. Nevertheless, a measure of impartiality would have gone into the process of selection of these senior electoral officers.
I was a little worried earlier this evening in case the idea got around outside the chamber that there was a contest to see how many of their experienced people each political party could get hired by the Chief Electoral Officer. The point we were trying to make was this: there is nothing wrong in being partisan or in having experience of the political process on behalf of a political party. But the Chief Electoral Officer has to work with whoever is selected as a returning officer, and it seems to me he should have some say in the selection. If the President of the Privy Council would accept this amendment, I could think of a person who has been for a number of years an organizer in the Liberal party and who would make a first-class returning officer. He has never behaved in a vicious manner; he has always acted in a positive and construc-

tive way, and he probably knows more about the election law in that province than does his returning officer.

Then how is it he is a
Liberal?

The fact that he has come up against honest competition might have helped. The election law is reviewed every eight or ten years. There is not a party in this chamber or outside which does not agree the time is long past due to place in the hands of a person in whom we all have confidence the responsibility for recommending the officers he would like to work with him. The Chief Electoral Officer might provide three choices to the Governor in Council. He might recommend two or three people after considering their abilities and holding a competition. Whoever is chosen, he will have had some say as to the calibre of the people who will fill these senior positions. If the Governor in Council, in its wisdom, was not satisfied with the recommendations, it could ask the Chief Electoral Officer to submit further names. So the point raised by the minister is met by the proposal in this amendment. We would in fact present an electoral law which finally provided for a new method of selecting the 264 people who will run and supervise our election procedures in the constituencies of Canada.
If it would make the amendment more acceptable, the word "shall" in the fourth line could be replaced by the word "may". The point is to provide an element of examination and selection by the Chief Electoral Officer prior to a recommendation to the Privy Council. We believe that here is an opportunity to make an improvement in the law, in a bipartisan manner, for the first time since 1962 or 1963-and if that would not be refreshing to the public of Canada, I do not know what would be. I urge hon. members in all quarters of the House carefully to consider this proposal.

Mr. Chairman, I can hardly believe there has been a more important bill before the Commons this session than the present measure, one which is concerned with a vital part of the democratic process. All of us have an interest in making sure it is the best statute we can possibly enact. As an important election official, a returning officer should be non-partisan in the performance of his duties and we should do our best to ensure that this will be the case.

With regard to the comments of the hon. member for St. Paul's and other hon. gentlemen in regard to the importance of being able to act quickly and effectively, this is perhaps

illustrated by the following figures indicating experience during the last six general election campaigns with respect to filling of vacancies in the two-week period on either side of the date the writ is issued. In 1957 there was one returning officer appointed in that period; in 1958 there were 17 returning officers appointed; in 1962 there were three; in 1963 there were 12; in 1965 there were four; in 1968 there were 14.
I think it is clear, particularly in view of the fairly strict qualifications in terms of residence and otherwise of returning officers set out later in the section, that this is a situation wherein there has to be some swiftness. In the proposal suggested in the amendment, which deals with advertising the vacancy, in the coming and going and putting of names, having them rejected, and so on, this swiftness does not exist.
I suggest that the amendment does not effectively deal with the fact that there is a need in each election campaign to act swiftly. The hon. member for Fraser Valley West commented that he had suffered no disadvantage from returning officers, whatever the existing system might be, and this seems to me the best answer. It has operated fairly and as the Chief Electoral Officer himself has said, this is the most efficient method.

Mr. Chairman, I have a very brief intervention. I would suggest that the President of the Privy Council, in consultation with the Chief Electoral Officer and his legal advisers, consider drafting a further subsection to cover the necessity for occasionally appointing returning officers in a crisis situation through the Governor in Council, subject to the procedure outlined in this amendment being pursued after the general election is completed. I am sure that such an amendment would not be beyond his inventiveness. Mr. Chairman, I can well understand why the NDP are sponsoring this amendment, it is because there is no chance of that party ever assuming power. In 1960 the present loyal opposition were quite sure they would maintain power and they made no suggestion along the lines of this amendment. It is unfortunate that, having reached a position so devoid of hope of ever being in power, they are now supporting this amendment. However, I say to them, "Take heart; this may not be the situation forever."

I intervene in this debate because I have heard it said, on this side of the House as well as on the other, that this amendment seems to be a rational one, on the assumption that the Chief Electoral Officer wants to be burdened with making this choice, supposedly through some sort of open competition. If he were to appoint a certain number of NDP'ers or Conservatives, there would be a holocaust of criticism from the other party, and this he does not want. Where is he going to find refuge? After all, it is the Chief Electoral Officer who is now guiding the bill, with the assistance of the President of the Privy Council; I do not think it is the other way around. He does not want to be saddled with this burden.
The suggestion was made that the final choice was that of the Governor in Council. Imagine a situation where the Chief Electoral Officer has made a judicious choice of returning officers, and yet the Governor in Council-the cabinet-rejects them. This would put an officer of Parliament in confrontation with the cabinet. The fact is that the Governor in Council does not have the final choice; such suggestion is a fallacy. The choice has to be entirely the responsibility of the Chief Electoral Officer, and he does not want this responsibility. Members of the party in power have, by chance, been elected returning officers and they have been good ones. No one has ever complained that they were inefficient or that they had done something wrong. I suggest we have had a good system and that no one has devised a better one, one that does not involve confrontation between the Chief Electoral Officer and the government of Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I have listened with great interest to the experienced and inexperienced views of a number of members who have spoken on this matter. I was particularly interested in the remarks made by the last speaker. He pointed out that since the system had worked rather well in the past, it should, if I understood him correctly, be continued. I was surprised at his remarks in view of the analogous situation described by the Minister of Justice in regard to the appointment of judges. No one wants judges appointed on a partisan basis. It has been suggested that a new system be devised whereby the bar associations recommend to the Governor in Council appointees to the bench. I do not think I have heard any disagreement from anybody to this proposal. The situation there is analogous to the one here.

This amendment suggests that the Chief Electoral Officer recommends one or two people to the Governor in Council. I cannot understand how any serious objection could be taken to this. As I say, it is similar to the proposal of the Minister of Justice in regard to the appointment of judges. I think it is a splendid idea and I cannot see why the governing party should object to it. However, under the present regime we have become accustomed to the attitude of the government that no member in any part of the House other than on the government side has any ideas of merit to put forward. There is never any disposition on the government side of the House to accept suggestions made by members in other quarters of the House.
The President of the Privy Council has very eloquently tried to explain that there might be a situation where there is no time to make an appointment. Personally, I cannot swallow this argument and I do not think anybody else can. All I can say is that the old motto of the Liberal party-power, patronage and perpetuity-has been eloquently exemplified by the President of the Privy Council and his cohorts.

Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to take up very much time. I do not think we are going to change the system one way or the other. I suppose in respect of the returning officer of a district 50 per cent of the names in urban ridings come from sitting members and 50 per cent from the other parties. In the rural ridings they all come from those who were lucky enough to win the previous election.
As I see it-and I have had experience of several elections-those people who happen to enumerate someone land up in the headquarters of the particular parties they want to land up in. I do not think we should waste any more time. We know this is going to be a partisan matter. I do not mind something being partisan if I know about it. I have prepared an amendment which, in my opinion, might satisfy everybody, if Parliament still trusts its judges. The act clearly states that if there is a doubt about the election of a candidate, it is always possible to ask for a judicial recount. We have enough confidence in the integrity of judges to assume that recounts are made honestly.
As the office of returning officer is extremely important since the result of an election depends upon him, his integrity must be above suspicion. Moreover, he must not be a recognized politician or a low-rate politician who has become famous through dubious election practices and who is being rewarded for his services by his party.
That is certainly possible, because I have seen it myself. That is why I have had to live through elections with returning officers whose ability was doubtful but whose political past was not.
Mr. Chairman, I suggest that if we have confidence in judges to make a judicial recount in an intelligent and honest manner, it would be normal when it comes to filling such an important office as that of returning officer to call upon the integrity and ability of judges.
It is also a fact that judges in a judicial district know many persons of impeccable integrity. They might therefore be better qualified to appoint returning officers. The governor in council would no longer have to rely on political say-so, tending to favour friends. Political affiliation should no longer be taken into account, but rather the fact that judges can best identify those who are involved in politics, when such an appointment has to be made.

I will start by admitting that my intimate knowledge of English grammar is scant, but the wording of the first part of subclause 2 seems to be, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre put it to me earlier, a bit lousy. It reads:
The office of a returning officer is not vacant unless he dies-
Who is "he"? Is it the office, or the returning officer? Is it the office that dies, or the returning officer? Surely the office does not die, but rather the individual. I mention the point in order to reflect the opinion of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, who is highly expert in the field of grammatical construction.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader

speechtext: I am advised that the phrase has been in the act for a considerable time and that there are virtually no precedents in this regard. Perhaps we can regard ourselves as having been fortunate.

The provision says that the Governor in Council may remove from office any returning officer who has at any time after his appointment been guilty of politically partisan conduct, whether or not in the course of the performance of his duties under this act. It seems to me it is obvious, and I think that the President of the Privy Council knows what it means. If the cabinet, or Governor in Council, found the man was partisan, he would be out; and if they found that whatever he did was proper, he would be in.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)

Mr. Chairman, I think it might be appropriate, particularly in reference to the point that has been raised, to bring the attention of members of the committee to the fact that this question was not lightly dealt with by the committee. Indeed, it occupied considerable time of the committee, particularly with respect to the onus which it places on the Chief Electoral Officer in being a final judge in this matter.

The final authority must be the Governor in Council, but the bill provides that the removal is on the basis of advice by the Chief Electoral Officer to the Governor in Council. Granted, the word is a permissive one; it says "may remove." I wonder if it would be wise to pass this paragraph without members of the committee being aware that in accepting the amendment we are perpetuating a system in our electoral act which places an area of judgment in the office of the Chief Electoral Officer, one that I do not particularly like to mention. I am certain that the officer in question does not particularly like to have this type of onus placed on his shoulders.
For their edification I would refer members of the committee to volume 8 of the proceedings of the Privileges and Elections Committee. I have never been able to figure out the paging of these things, but it says 8:20, 8:21, 8:22 and 8:23. This question might be considered the next time the act is to be amended, even if it is in ten years' time.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to ask a question of the President of the Privy Council to find out if in the event of a returning officer being removed, particularly in the case of alleged political activity following his appointment to office, he has any appeal procedures open to him.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I understand that the practice referred to here has been carried on for nearly 20 years under the discretionary powers conferred upon the Chief Electoral Officer. What we are doing in this section is putting into the statute what has been practised heretofore.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to suggest an amendment to sub-
[The Chairman.]
clause 10, to delete in lines 22 and 23 the words "mentioned in schedule III". What I seek to accomplish can be done this way or it can be done with respect to a particular constituency. It can be done by seeking to amend schedule III when we get to it, but we thought it would be easier to do it this way because there may be other constituencies in the same situation. I present this amendment on behalf of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni who was concerned about this matter because of the geography of his constituency. Regretfully, he had to enter hospital today and will be there for a few days.
As the President of the Privy Council has said, the opportunity for the Chief Electoral Officer to make these decisions has existed for some time and has worked very well. But we are now embarking on a new venture in the Canada Elections Act, namely, proxy voting. Under the proxy voting structure, in certain constituencies it was felt necessary to give the elector an opportunity to apply to the returning officer or to one of the two or more election clerks who may be appointed for the constituencies named in the schedule. Comox-Alberni is not mentioned in the schedule. It is one of the constituencies within which there shall be a nomination day or polling day. The hon. member for Comox-Alberni says this is not really necessary because of the communication that exists between constituencies with regard to ballot-boxes and the like, but he felt it was necessary because of the scattered nature of the riding.
If we were to remove the reference here to schedule III, it would permit the Chief Electoral Officer to use his discretionary powers in designated constituencies to appoint an election clerk in addition to the regular election clerk already available. This would make things easier for constituents of Comox-Alberni, many of whom are fishermen and prospectors who may wish to exercise their right to the proxy vote. There may be other constituencies falling in the same category, so we felt it better to raise the matter at his juncture. Perhaps it is appropriate to do so at this time because it is close to ten o'clock and unless it is immediately acceptable to the President of the Privy Council it affords us the opportunity to hold it over. This is the reasoning behind it. It would be of great assistance to other constituencies as well as Comox-Alberni.

That clause 11 be amended by:
(a)	In subclause 1 after the word "more" In line 29, adding the words 'or any municipal district, or part thereof, served by postal walk.'

I move this amendment on behalf of my colleague for Fraser Valley West whose suburban constituency, in common with that of other hon. members of the House, in part is still considered rural. There are portions not incorporated into a city or town even though the population is 5,000 or more. These one or more portions are in a municipal district and are looked upon as rural districts. One of the ramifications would be appointing two enumerators per poll, rather than one. That will probably allow a better job of enumera-

tion to be done in those places which because of their density of population would otherwise probably be part of a city or incorporated town with a population of 5,000 or more, as defined in the act.

I hope members will agree that this amendment will be useful in a large number of constituencies where there are areas, bordering on cities or towns, which are still municipal or rural districts.

Mr. Chairman, we have an amendment to subclause 8, for two reasons. One reason, which is not the most important, is that we consider there is a real conflict in this clause. Paragraph (b) of subclause 8 states:
after the twenty-eighth day before polling day, delete from the registry any registered party that
Then subparagraph (ii) states:
did not, on the twenty-eighth day before polling day at the election, have candidates officially nominated in at least seventy-five electoral districts of Canada.
Mr. Chairman, we believe there is a serious conflict here because in all but 21 constituencies nomination day closes 21 days before polling day, not 28 days before polling day. Any political party in this House or any political party which might be in existence and which is not now in this House could quite readily nominate 75 candidates in that seven-day period between the twenty-first day and the twenty-eighth day. In fact, this has been known to happen. In previous years parties now represented in this House deliberately planned nominating conventions in a short space of time in an effort to create a political impact on the public in a province or in a given part of Canada. I throw that out as an example of what has happened in the past and might happen in the future.
I suppose the point I make could be thrown out by saying that a political party would only need to advance its mass nominations by seven days in order to have sufficient candidates nominated before 28 days before polling day. But the essential point is, so far as the conflict in the figure of 75 and the number of days before polling day in which they must be nominated, is concerned, that there is a seven-day period during which candidates may still be nominated by a political party, but in the course of those seven days, the difference between 28 and 21 days, they will lose the right to have their party affiliation on the ballot even though they may have been before that time legally registered as a political party under the terms of the act. I put that point forward for the consideration of the President of the Privy Council and mem-

bers of this committee, to see whether there is some way in which we can solve the problem.
[DOT] (10:20 p.m.)
Now 1 would like to come to the second and more pertinent point of my argument regarding the necessity for an amendment. The Standing Committee report, under recommendation No. 29, recommended that political parties in Canada wishing to endorse candidates for election to the House of Commons should be registered with the Chief Electoral Officer. In addition, any new party that wishes to be identified on the ballot paper must have candidates in at least 10 per cent of the total number of electoral districts of Canada. If my memory serves me correctly, that was a unanimous recommendation of the Standing Committee. The government in its wisdom chose not to agree with that recommendation and inserted the figure 75 instead of the figure recommended by the committee, which was 26.4 or, to round out the figure, 27, in order to retain the privilege of having the party affiliation designated on the ballot.
I appreciate to some extent the arguments put forward by the President of the Privy Council and others on second reading, that there could be a danger once this country makes provision to control election expenses, and that there would be some necessity for making safeguards to prevent frivolity of political parties such as the "rhinoceros party'' or other such parties that are formed overnight or a few days before a general election in order to secure public funds.
I submit in all sincerity that the political affiliation on the ballot of a recognized political party which has properly adhered to or abided by all the regulations of this bill should be completely separate from any consideration regarding public funds or control of election expenses. I am fully prepared to agree that there is a need for a higher level of safeguard regarding the expenditure of public funds than just fielding 27 candidates, and I would not argue on that score with any member of the House. However, it seems to me that a new political party or one that is presently in existence but is not represented in this chamber-and there but for the grace of God go any of our parties two or three elections from now when one of our parties may be in the position of having less than 12 members in the House-might not have 75 candidates nominated 28 days before election day and would thus lose the privilege that they may have held for a number of years.
June 16, 1970

It seems to me there was a great deal of unanimity of feeling among members of the committee that it is an essential addition to our election law that the party affiliation be designated on the ballot. All members of the committee wanted to ensure that there be minimal obstruction to retaining that privilege. Therefore, my amendment is as follows:
That clause 13 be amended by deleting from subclause 8 paragraph (b) (ii) in line 26, the words "seventy five" and substituting therefor the words "twenty seven".
First, this complies with the unanimous recommendation of the Standing Committee which spent more hours on this bill than will committee of the whole and discussed this matter all the way from 75 down to 10 candidates in the field. In fact, I think it was even suggested that you should have 100 candidates in the field in order to retain your party affiliation on the ballot. But the committee felt that aside from any consideration of public expenditure and control of election expenses, the safeguards should be minimal so that any party with a semblance of credibility could have its party affiliation appear on the ballot.
A party that attempted to attain party affiliation on the ballot in a frivolous manner, or in a manner that would cause our electoral process to lose the esteem in which it is held, could have much difficulty in fielding even 27 candidates. I am sure many of us can think of events in past history where groups of that sort attempted to demean our electoral process or to participate in it in a frivolous manner, but they failed to field even 10, 12 or 15 candidates. I do not think 27 is too low a figure for any group to form a party, and such a party should have the privilege of having its party affiliation appear on the ballot, provided that party abides by the other provisions of the Elections Act.
I plead with the President of the Privy Council and other hon. members who spoke on second reading that there is no reason to connect this figure with control of election expenses or expenditure of public funds for electoral purposes. All of us are proud of our political affiliation. There may be times when we are not so proud in that respect, but we do not talk about them. The least we can do is make it easier for other Canadians to have that pride.
Members of a party now in this House may face great misfortune in years to come, and at that time they would still want their party affiliation to appear on the ballot. I hope the President of the Privy Council changes his
Canada Elections Act
mind a little bit, say by 40 degrees if not 180 degrees. If he cannot be persuaded to accept the figure of 27, let him look again at the 75 figure, because any party can have difficulty fielding 75 candidates in seven days.

Unless I am mistaken, the passage of clause 13 will mean that each candidate of a recognized party will be identified with his party. At the last election, the Speaker of the House of Commons ran as an independant and, since we have decided to indicate the names of the political parties, we have done away with any reference to the address and the occupation of the candidate. In my opinion, perhaps we should consider the possibility of making an exception in the case of the Speaker and enter him as being politically unaffiliated in order to prevent someone with the same name from running as an independent candidate in the same riding.
All political parties have realized the necessity of omitting the political affiliation of the Speaker whose name and occupation should appear instead on the ballot paper.

My mind is open on this amendment and I gather the distinguished President of the Privy Council's mind is open as well, which surprises me a little. When we were discussing this question in committee there was some concern that it would permit easy access to the formation of regional parties which would be coloured as such in terms of their impact on the Canadian scene. There were several excellent reasons why the figure of 75 was suggested. While this particular section is stood overnight I would ask hon. members to think about the distinct possibility of the danger inherent in lowering the number from 75 to 27. If the number were 27 it is quite possible, for example, that we in the Mari-times could become totally fed-up with the rest of Canada and would form our own party to sit in the House. I do not think that lends itself to Canadian unity. If by the suggestion that is what we are attempting to encourage, whether we express it or not I think we should give some thought to it.

Clause 14, subclause 1-Persons qualified as electors.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, to bring this amendment clearly to the attention of the committee, the basic qualifications of electors are changed in a fundamental way. First, the minimum voting age is reduced from 21 to 18 and, second, it is made perfectly clear, subject only to subclause 3, that only those who are Canadian citizens will be qualified to vote in a Canadian federal election.

Mr. Chairman, I have
already dealt with this question which I feel is important and which the President of the Privy Council has already answered. However, it is essential that I raise the matter

again and that I express the views of many of my colleagues.
We grant to young Canadians the right to vote at 18 and to run in an election. If we grant them that right, we must also entrust them with the resulting responsabili-ties.
The President of the Privy Council has explained-and I fully agree with him on that point-that the fact of lowering the legal age from 21 to 18 years of age is a provincial prerogative, as everybody knows. It would be logical, since several very serious reasons justify such a step, for the President of the Privy Council to obtain from the government the assurance that at one of the next federal-provincial conferences a dialogue will take place with the provinces to have them all reduce the legal age from 21 to 18. This is very important.
In fact, if a young man is entitled to vote or to run as a candidate at 18 or 19 years of age, he could, for instance, be prosecuted for libel, and his father's responsibility would then be involved. Many similar cases might occur.
In my opinion, logic and common sense require that the legal age be set at 18. Young people of 18 and over should be granted the rights that will come with their majority if they are given the franchise and allowed to be run as candidates in elections.
I know that the federal government cannot put such a clause in the act; however, I do think that I am expressing the wish of .many of my colleagues when I ask that the government take the initiative of starting a dialogue with the provinces in order that the legal age may be set at 18 as soon as possible in all provinces.

In speaking about this question I want to make it perfectly clear that I am not joining the crowd to my far left who are opponents of the Senate. I will join their crusade when I am 74J years old and root for the abolition of the Senate. I think for too long in this country we have downgraded the Upper House and have not really taken cognizance of the fact that our Parliament is made up of two chambers. The Senate is an integral part of Parliament. We have been led to this conclusion by the expression "Member of Parliament" which leads us to think only of members of the Lower House. Our United States friends have done exactly the same thing. When they talk of a Congressman they think of a member of the House of Representatives, whereas they ought to be thinking of both their Houses. My amendment seeks to give full credit and precedence to our Upper House, as is done in the United Kingdom in the case of the House of Lords.

I was not clear as to the intent of the amendment moved earlier by the hon. member for Matane. Our amendment is to subclause 2. It would have the effect of delaying for a fairly short period, for a year or perhaps two years, the provision whereby British subjects who have taken out Canadian citizenship cannot vote, and thus enable these recent British subjects to cast their ballot if they meet the other qualifications of residence. However, once the act comes into force British subjects arriving in Canada would have to serve the required five years and secure their Canadian citizenship before being eligible to cast their ballot in a federal election.
It has already been represented to me by some British subjects who have arrived in Canada that one of the things they were told before departing for their new home was that after one year's residence they would be eligible to vote in elections in Canada. One person who made representations to me both by mail and by telephone lives in Ontario, and he told me that although this would not have prevented his coming to Canada, the information that had been given to him would be falsified as a result of this change in electoral law. He submitted, and I agreed, that those coming to Canada have every right to know before arriving what their rights and privileges are in this country from the very day they arrive.
I want to make it quite plain that there is no misunderstanding here. We in this party completely agree that there should no longer be in our electoral law any discrimination as to the eligibility to cast ballots as between

British subjects and those of other racial or ethnic origins. This has to stop in modern Canada. However, those British subjects who arrived in Canada between June 26, 1967, and the day on which this act comes into force should still retain their right to vote as British subjects. Those who arrive in Canada subsequent to the coming into force of this legislation will know beforehand that they must serve the five-year period and become Canadian citizens before being given the federal franchise.
However, I think we should be fair to those who arrived in Canada between June 26, 1967, and the day this act comes into force, which might be next month or next year. These people could number 60,000 to 70,000, if the immigration pattern has remained fairly constant. They should not be disenfranchised because when they arrived in Canada the legislation had not been amended. Therefore, I should like to move the following motion. I regret I have only one copy. I have rewritten the amendment because I received better legal advice in the last few minutes than I did yesterday. I move:
That clause 14 he amended by deleting subclause 3 on page 24 and substituting therefor the following:
"(3) Every British subject, other than a Canadian citizen, who
(a)	was qualified as an elector immediately prior to the coming into force of the provisions of this act referred to in subsection 2 of section 119, and
(b)	has not, since that date, ceased to be ordinarily resident in Canada, is deemed to be qualified as an elector.
As I say, I am sorry I have only one copy. In view of this I would ask the President of the Privy Council and other members of the committee to sleep on this amendment overnight and to consider giving fair treatment to those British subjects who have arrived in Canada since June 26, 1967, and before the act is proclaimed. They will still be eligible to vote without having to wait the five-year period, but if a British subject arrives in Canada after this bill comes into force he would have to wait the five-year period before he has the federal franchise.
[DOT] (10:50 p.m.)

May I point out to my friend that anyone who emigrates to Canada, be he a British subject or otherwise, knows he will be subject to any new law that might be passed in Canada. What the hon. member is suggesting is similar to the following situation. If I were to emigrate to Canada because there was no military service here, and then
June 16, 1970	COMMONS
suddenly this Parliament decided to vote for conscription in Canada, I might say exactly what the hon. member is trying to say about British subjects being betrayed. In this situation I would have emigrated to Canada because there was no military service and I could say that I was not subject to such a law because when I came to Canada I was told by the immigration officer that there was no military service here. This could be an analogous situation. I am sure people do not come to Canada with only this incentive.

Mr. Chairman, I would normally accept the proposition that these matters stand, but I understand we did agree to some of them. Normally I would have forgone the opportunity to put forward an idea in respect of this question, but it is close to the time at which we have agreed to see the clock and it might be worth while to put something else before the committee so that it may also be considered overnight. If the amendment of the hon. member for Matane should carry, it would not, I submit, remove the matter of privilege or relief-if one should want to put it another way-in terms of the eligibility to vote, because that situation will still prevail not as a result of the Elections Act but as a result of the Citizenship Act.
Under that act we do discriminate, as I understand it, against the male sex in favour of the female sex in certain circumstances. Normally a person must wait five years before applying for Canadian citizenship, but if a woman who has emigrated to Canada marries a Canadian citizen she has only to wait one year before she can apply for Canadian citizenship. I think that if the government wishes to deal fairly with this matter and bring it up to date, it should consider eliminating the five-year period and instituting a more reasonable period, perhaps one year, so that all people will have equality before the law in terms of citizenship and the right to vote.
While I generally agree with the proposition that equality before the law should not be based on having a privileged position, nonetheless there is a matter which I think should be raised, namely, that it is unfair to a group of people to remove from them a right
